ROUYN DISASTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were shocked to learn this morning of the dreadful fire which broke out last night at Rouyn, a city in the constituency I have the honour to represent in this house.
Fortunately, the anxiety of the citizens was not heightened by any loss of life.
Many families have not only sustained severe losses but are now homeless. At noon, I was informed that losses will total well over a million dollars.
May I, Mr. Speaker, tender my deepest sympathy to all the victims of this disaster, be they landlords or tenants, and may I also congratulate the dauntless firemen and citizens of Rouyn who now have the fire entirely under control.

subtopic: GRANTS TO POLICE AND FIRE DEPARTMENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: GRANTS TO POLICE AND FIRE DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked a question about civil defence, having regard to proposals put forward in the Ontario legislature by the attorney general. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has given notice of an inquiry of the ministry as to the same matter. I am glad to make a brief statement in reply to both questions.
Some time ago Major General F. F. Worthington was appointed civil defence adviser. As such he has been working with the various federal departments and agencies that might be concerned, and has visited the United States, Great Britain, and other countries, to bring our information up to date as to what is being done or proposed in those countries.
The vast extent of Canada and the nature of the problems involved in civil defence make it clear that suitable safeguards require close working arrangements among the various
agencies of government, federal, provincial and municipal, as well as transportation and communication services, and national and local organizations. Moreover, many of the matters relating to civil defence fall within the ordinary jurisdiction of the provinces and municipalities of Canada, which are responsible for municipal services such as fire fighting.
On my instruction Major General Worthington visited all the provinces, and at each place saw either the premier or a member of the cabinet, at which time arrangements were discussed in a general way. I should like to say that all provinces showed a most co-operative attitude. These preliminary discussions are being followed up.
In considering civil defence, it is apparent that one of the actions which would be desirable would be that the couplings and attachments of fire equipment be standardized as far as possible. While some progress has been made, I am informed that there are no less than two hundred types of 2J-inch fire hose coupling having either different threads or outside diameter which would make it impossible, or at least more difficult, for the fire equipment of one locality to be used in another. This is an objective which could be attained only over a period of time by the provinces agreeing on certain standards and working towards them. Clearly it is in the general interest of the people in the various parts of Canada that fire equipment be capable of being used in neighbouring municipalities.
Beyond these general discussions, no arrangements have yet been made with any of the provinces. Until today I had not seen the legislation proposed by the Ontario legislature. Of course I have not made and do not make any comment on that measure.

speechtext: As of February 15, 1949, how many Canadian army personnel have been qualified as parachutists (a) of the P.P.C.L.I.; (b) of other units?

subtopic: PARACHUTISTS
speechtext:
As is well known, it is not the practice here or in the United Kingdom to give the strength and other detailed information about individual units of the armed forces. If the information were to be given about one unit, there would be no reason for withholding it about others, and thus the entire battle order and fighting strength, which are matters any prospective enemy would take a great deal of trouble to find out, would be disclosed. Even though individual figures may not have any immediate significance, the fact that some were given and others withheld would give information or create ground for speculation.
Changes in the strength or locations of individual units might have the utmost significance. It may be interesting to observe that in the soviet union the giving of such information as is sought here is a crime punishable by ten to twenty years in prison. Few figures could be given which would be of greater interest to the only possible aggressor than the information sought in answer to these two questions.
Accordingly it is not in the public interest to give this or similar information in reply to this and the next question. However, I shall be glad to give the hon. member the information for his own private use, if he wants it.

subtopic: PACIFIC PAY
PACIFIC PAY
speechtext:
1.	What action has been taken by the Department of National Defence with reference to the representations of the Hong Kong veterans for Pacific pay, as contained in their brief presented to the Veterans Affairs committee June 17. 1948, and forwarded by the committee to the Minister of National Defence for consideration?
2.	If no action has been taken as yet, will favourable consideration be given to the representations of these veterans?

subtopic: PACIFIC PAY
speechtext:
The question of giving Pacific pay to the members of the Hong Kong forces has been under consideration for some time. Under P.C. 3593 of May 17, 1945, authority was granted for the payment of "Japanese campaign pay" to members of the Canadian army Pacific forces, effective June 1, 1945, and to begin from the date of departure from Canada. The main reason for this provision was that our forces would be acting in close association with the forces of the United States, which had a different pay structure from ours, and which, unlike the Canadian pay structure, made express provision for foreign service pay. The order did not cover Canadians who had fought in the Pacific, including the Hong Kong force, the Kiska force and members of the R.C.A.F. and others who had taken part in the active operations in the Pacific.
However, representations were received from members of parliament and others that members of the Hong Kong force who had suffered so much should receive the same entitlement as members of the Canadian army Pacific forces. This has led the government

to consider the matter on different occasions and in the light of difficulties which favourable action might create. Generally speaking it is a good rule that no pay provision should be made retroactive so as to include a class that had not been covered. The circumstances here, however, were so different that it was felt that others could not properly regard this as opening the way for other retroactive adjustments.	.
In principle the matter was decided by the government some time ago, and I am glad to be able to announce now that the terms of the original order will be extended so as to make members of the Hong Kong forces eligible for Pacific pay until two months after return of such members to Canada.

subtopic: NIAGARA FRONTIER COMMUTERS
NIAGARA FRONTIER COMMUTERS
speechtext:
1.	What action is being taken to collect arrears of income tax in the Niagara river border from commuters who work in the United States?
2.	What demands for immediate payment have been made for income tax arrears?
3.	What is being done regarding arrears of income tax owing by the members of the Niagara frontier commuters association in these matters?

subtopic: NIAGARA FRONTIER COMMUTERS
speechtext:
1.	Taxpayers who are residents of Canada hut receive income as a result of services rendered in the United States are taxable under the Canadian law but are allowed to offset against Canadian tax payable any taxes paid to the United States on income derived from sources therein. The collection action involved is to forward an assessment notice and two collection letters within a specified period unless payment or arrangements for payment are made in the interval. If payment is not received or arrangements made, further collection action as provided by the Income Tax Act is considered and, if deemed advisable, applied.
2.	Demands for immediate payment have been made only in those cases where the taxpayer had omitted to communicate with the district income tax office and to arrange for settlement of his outstanding taxes. Even at this stage, should the taxpayer make a suggestion regarding payment, it would be given consideration by the department and the demand lifted if the proposal is considered reasonable.
3.	Members of Niagara frontier commuters association are taxable if residents of Canada, and they are treated in a similar manner to other Canadian taxpayers who may have fallen in arrears in respect of their obligations.

PROVISION FOR MORNING SITTINGS UNTIL CERTAIN
subtopic: MEASURES DISPOSED OF

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR MORNING SITTINGS UNTIL CERTAIN
subtopic: MEASURES DISPOSED OF
speechtext:
That on and after Friday, March 18, 1949, until the following resolutions and the legislation based thereon be disposed of by this house, viz.: (a) the resolution for a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war; (b) the resolution for a measure to amend the Agricultural Products Act to extend the operation of the act for a period of one year; (c) the resolution to amend the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act to provide authority for advances to the corporation by way of loan out of the consolidated revenue fund and to extend the time of operation of the act; (d) the resolution for a measure to provide for the

continuance in force of the Foreign Exchange Control Act until sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament commencing in the year 1951; the house shall meet at 11 o'clock in the morning of each sitting day and that in addition to the usual intermission at 6 o'clock there shall also be an intermission every day from 1 to 3 o'clock p.m.; and further that on Saturday, March 26, 1949, the house shall meet at 11 o'clock a.m. and the order of business and procedure shall be the same as on Friday, March 25, 1949.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reasons for this motion are the same as I gave for the motion I put before the house on March 11, to give priority to these resolutions and the legislation based thereon. The present legislation with respect to the matters described in paragraphs (a), (c) and (d) would expire on the 27th of March if not extended by parliament before that date. The legislation described in paragraph (b), the Agricultural Products Act, would expire on March 31 if not extended before that date.
Hon. members will realize that all the steps required for these resolutions and the legislation based thereon provide many opportunities for debate. On each one there is opportunity for debate on the motion that you, sir, leave the chair. There is opportunity for debate in committee after you leave the chair. There is opportunity for debate on the second reading of the bill, in committee of the whole when the bill is being considered clause by clause, and on the third reading of the bill. There are four of these measures, and I indicated it might be desirable to consider a fifth, namely, the consolidation of the bonuses or supplementary payments being made to mail carriers on a contract basis. As one can see, there would be some twenty or more opportunities for debate.
The debate on one subject was begun on Monday and has been continued ever since, but as yet, we have gone through only one of the five stages provided for by each of these resolutions. On Friday last when making the motion I stated that the government believed it to be its duty to make every possible effort to have these measures considered by parliament and disposed of so that they would not expire by mere lapse of time, and that each member would have an opportunity of taking his responsibility in respect thereto and expressing his views in this house.
The motion now before the house would add some twenty-two hours to the time available after today for further consideration of these matters. The time available otherwise would amount to thirty-nine hours; by this motion we are adding something more than fifty per cent to the time available for the
House of Commons
consideration of these measures. I recommend to the house this further effort to deal with matters which are evidently of great interest, whatever one's view about them may be. I believe the provision of this additional time will be a demonstration that the members of this house do intend to discharge their responsibilities in regard to these matters.
Hon. members will see that this motion is drafted in such a way that it will no longer be operative if these resolutions and the legislation based thereon are disposed of before present legislation expires; the effect of the motion will disappear and we shall return to the standing orders. Under these conditions I trust that it will be the feeling of all members of the house that this order should be made.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR MORNING SITTINGS UNTIL CERTAIN
subtopic: MEASURES DISPOSED OF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to oppose the resolution. In indicating support of this proposal to increase the time available for discussion of the subject matters referred to, I think it should be clearly understood that there is a way in which any possibility of delay could have been avoided from the outset, and can be avoided now.
The Prime Minister has said that whether or not one favours these measures, they are regarded by the members as matters of some importance. The main point at issue is not the measure that is contemplated, but the way it is done. The main point at issue is whether we are to act as a parliament and deal with legislation by bills properly presented, or whether we are to carry forward these dictatorial orders.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a short reply to this further lesson on propriety of procedure in this house which the new leader of the Progressive Conservative party has been dinning into our ears ever since the beginning of the session.
I would remind the followers of the new leader of their attitude only two years ago when they were pounding their desks just as vigorously in applause of the remarks of one who was suggesting that in dealing with this kind of legislation we should follow the procedure which was followed in the British House of Commons. That we did last year by bringing in a bill with a schedule of I'Mr. Drew.]
orders attached to it. Then hon. members opposite complained because there were fifty-seven orders and there were not to be fifty-seven times five opportunities for obstructive filibustering debate.
This year, as last year, though it was not necessarily the best one, we followed the procedure that was recommended by hon. members on the other side because we hoped that by that means the merits of matters would be considered and we would have done with this waste of time in futile discussions about procedure. I have attended meetings of other deliberative bodies and have seen just the same tactics adopted and the same waste of time by those who were obstructing consideration of the real merits of issues. I do not need to tell this house from what quarter those tactics came. Here in this house we took ten days on the proposal for the union of Newfoundland with Canada. Hon. gentlemen on the other side asserted in the most formal terms that there was nothing they desired more than the union of Newfoundland with Canada, but they said that the procedure was wrong. This parliament, about the respect of whose privileges and authority they have been clamouring ever since we came back here on January 26, was not competent to deal with the problem. It could not be dealt with, according to my hon. friends opposite, until this parliament had obtained Mr. Duplessis' permission. For three days now these hon. gentlemen have been asserting that they are not opposed to the continuation of rent control, and that they are not opposed to the continuation of steel control. But, they say, the procedure is not the one that should have been adopted; instead of twenty opportunities for filibustering debates, they argued, we should have given them four times twelve more opportunities for it. That it is expedient to present a measure to provide for the continuance in force of the Foreign Exchange Control Act until sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament commencing in the year 1951.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill which this resolution seeks leave to introduce is a bill which provides merely for the extension of the Foreign Exchange Control Act, adopted by this house in 1946, for a further two-year

period. No doubt the house will recall that, when the original measure was introduced in and passed by this house, it contained no limitation as to time. In another place, however, an amendment was offered, and was accepted by the government, providing that the act would lapse sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament in the year 1949. That amendment was agreed to by the house, and the termination provision is incorporated in section 73 of the present act.
The effect of this new bill, when it is enacted, will be to postpone the termination date for a period expiring sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament in the year 1951; in other words, an effective extension of some two years. Otherwise the provisions of the present Foreign Exchange Control Act are to be left unchanged. The normal British constitutional procedure, under which acts of parliament remain in force until they are repealed by parliament, has a good deal to recommend it; but in view of the legislative history which I have outlined, the government felt the same practice should be followed here, and that a measure should be introduced extending the provisions of the act for a further period. The idea behind the time limit was, of course, to ensure that the measure would come up for review after a specified interval, and parliament would have the opportunity of determining at that time whether the legislation should be continued as being necessary and desirable.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has indicated, we have nearly reached the end of the time when the existing measure will expire, and parliament must now review the situation and determine whether or not the provisions of the present act should be extended, whether or not it is desirable and necessary to continue this act. Speaking for the government, I may say that I have no hesitation in stating that, in view of prevailing conditions in the field of trade and commerce, and currency conditions throughout the world, we would not feel justified in suggesting to parliament that it is no longer necessary to exercise control over Canada's foreign exchange transactions.
When this measure was originally introduced it was recognized, of course, that the world outlook was very uncertain, and that Canada was in a very exposed position. It was recognized that we were particularly vulnerable to the impact of conditions originating abroad both because of the great importance of our foreign trade, and on account of our normal dependence on exports to the United Kingdom and certain other European countries, whose economies had been pretty seriously weakened by the war,
Foreign Exchange Control to pay for a very large proportion of our imports from the United States. The second factor exposing us to influences abroad was, and continues to be, our very large international indebtedness, particularly to the United States. Those were the main conditions which led the government to seek power to continue under legislative authority the operation of the exchange control which had originally been enforced at the very outbreak of the war.
The experience of the past two years has,
I think, served to confirm and reinforce the views which were then held, and adopted by this house, regarding the necessity of a measure of this kind. If anything, I think it is fair to say that we under-estimated the international economic difficulties of the post-war period, and the length of time and the degree of effort that would be required to overcome the distortions of war, and get the world back on its feet. The international flow of goods between the western hemisphere and Europe has been maintained, as the house is only too well aware, largely by extraordinary measures, such as credits extended by the United States and ourselves, and is now dependent to a very important extent on grants and loans from the United States government under ECA. The impact on Canada of these payment difficulties experienced by our customers was, as I have indicated, recognized in the debate which took place on this measure about two and a half years ago, but I think it has been realized much more clearly in the time which has since elapsed.
I do not suppose that the members of the house need to be reminded of the sharp decline which took place in our exchange reserves in 1947, or of the measures which the government found it necessary to take at that time to restore the situation. In the course of 1947 our official reserves of gold and United States dollars diminished from $1,250 million to approximately $500 million in the middle of November, and to a low of $461 million by the middle of December, 1947. A combination of two factors was mainly responsible for that fall in our reserves. The first, of course, was the unexpectedly slow rate of European recovery which led to a very much more rapid utilization of the Canadian loan to the United Kingdom than had originally been anticipated, and secondly, the very high level of prosperity and capital development in Canada which led to an unprecedented flow of imports from the United States, and the virtual elimination of the surplus in our current account balance of payments.
I am sure that members on all sides of the house will have noted with satisfaction the

As the facts regarding the record of our exchange transactions during the year have recently been made public in the annual report of the foreign exchange control board, which was tabled a few days ago, I think that in my remarks today I only need to refer to a few of the highlights.
Our official gold and United States dollar reserves rose from $502 million at the beginning of the year to $998 million at the end of the year. In this improvement of $496 million the sum of $150 million was not earned, but represents the proceeds of a loan on a bond issue which we sold to three American insurance companies last summer.
I am not going to suggest for a moment, of course, that all the credit for this improvement in our exchange position is due to government policies, but I do assert that those policies, both negative and positive, which were adopted to deal with our exchange difficulties, have been highly successful, and that the major part of the improvement which has taken place has been due to the adoption of those policies.
I referred a moment ago to negative and positive policies. The negative policies, of course, as the house appreciates, have been the import controls and the travel restrictions, which have resulted in a substantial curtailment of purchases in the United States, and of travel in that country. I think even more emphasis should be placed on the positive measures, including encouragement of exports to the United States under the direction of my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the development of Canadian tourist income with the valuable assistance of the Canadian co-operation project of the American moving picture industry, and the assistance to the gold mining industry. On the trade side, members of the house will be aware that we managed to reduce our merchandise trade deficit with the United States from $918 million in 1947 to only $284 million in 1948.
That, I think, was a truly remarkable achievement; and it is particularly gratifying to note that of this improvement of some $634 million as much as $465 million was due to increased exports to the United States and only $169 million to reduction of imports from that country. Percentagewise the increase in our exports to the United States was no less than 44 per cent; and notwithstanding the increasingly severe restrictions imposed against certain of our exports by a good many other foreign countries, the total value of our exports to all countries was higher in 1948 than in 1947, to be exact $3,110 million in 1948 as compared with $2,812


million in 1947, or an over-all increase of nearly 11 per cent. In this respect I may say our experience differed from that of the United States. The exports of that country to the world as a whole fell from over $15-3 billion in 1947 to about $12-6 billion in 1948, a decrease of nearly 18 per cent.
As I have said, o'Ur reserves of gold and United States dollars at the end of 1948 amounted to approximately $1 billion. That sounds like a pretty large figure, but in relation to our needs it is less than we had before the outbreak of war. At that time, that is to say in 1939, Canada had gold and United States dollar reserves amounting to approximately $400 million. In comparing the present figure of approximately $1 billion one must also bear in mind the very great increase that has taken place since that time in commodity prices, and also the very considerable increase which has occurred in the physical volume of our international trade and all other transactions against which reserves of this kind are held. One method of conveying these factors would be this. In 1939 our reserves were $400 million and our total imports $750 million; in other words we held reserves sufficient to pay for over six months' imports. We now hold reserves of approximately $1 billion and are importing at the rate of about $2,600 million, so as a consequence our reserves are sufficient to pay for somewhat less than five months' imports.
But perhaps the chief characteristic of the present situation as it affects our exchange arrangements is the uncertainty which surrounds the international trade outlook. Hon. members are well aware, of course, of our continued dependence upon United Kingdom and other western European markets to take some of our main export products and to provide us with exchange with which we can satisfy and pay for our imports from the United States. Notwithstanding the shift in imports to the United States I indicated a moment ago, which took place last year, the group of countries consisting of the United Kingdom and the rest of the sterling area and other countries participating in the European recovery program took 42 per cent of our exports in 1948.

We all appreciate that the government's decision to raise the exchange value of the Canadian dollar by ten per cent in July, 1946, had the effect of reducing the price of gold in Canada from $38.50 to $35 an ounce; and it is true that that reduction in price came at a very difficult time for the gold-mining industry, which was faced with rising costs and reduced profit margins. But I want to say this. So far as this government is concerned, the main economic policies of the country-those policies like the exchange rate policy which affect the well-being and the standard of living of the people of Canada-are not going to be determined to suit the convenience of any single economic interest, whether that interest is the gold-mining industry, the stock promoters, the wheat farmers, the manufacturers or any other single group. The main economic policies of this government are going to be determined in the light of the interests of the community as a whole, and not those of any single group.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, let me say this. The gold mining industry has, naturally, just as much claim to consideration as has any other group in this country; and the government and this house have recognized that claim in tangible form. The gold-mining industry, as everybody knows, tends to have a normal cycle of prosperity which is exactly opposite to that of most industries. When business conditions are active and there is an upward pressure on prices, costs go up while the price of their product, gold, does not do so. On the other hand, it frequently happens that, when other businesses are depressed, the costs of gold production go down, and since the price remains the same the margin of profit is of necessity increased. All of that is of course the logic of a monetary system which is based on gold. However, it is cold comfort to the gold-mining industry, at a time when other industries are very profitable and it is not, to think back to the days when the situation was reversed. Consequently last year the government recommended and this parliament approved a measure under which each gold mine is compensated for part of the increase in its costs of production above a certain level. I have no doubt that some of my hon. friends will want to remind us that Canada got into exchange difficulties in 1947, and that it was necessary for the government and parliament to take certain action, including import and travel restrictions to which I have referred, in order to improve our position. This is true, of course. But let me remind the house that even in 1947 we did not have a deficit in our over-all balance of payments on current account. On the contrary, we had a

surplus-excluding exports of goods financed by official relief contributions-amounting to $50 million. Our exchange difficulties arose, as I have indicated on other occasions, because some of our principal customers were not able to pay us in cash for all our exports, and in what I contend was a self-interested effort to aid their recovery we extended large amounts of credit to them. In 1948 we achieved an over-all balance of payments- excluding relief shipments-in excess of $450 million, an improvement of over $400 million, a record figure for a peacetime year. That compares with $50 million in 1947 and $350 million in 1946. It is true that some of this surplus was achieved as a result of import and travel restrictions to which I have referred and which the government is pledged to remove as soon as possible. But even without these restrictions we would undoubtedly have had a very substantial over-all current account surplus. Some relaxations have been made in these restrictions, but the restrictions have been maintained to the extent that they have for the same reason that the drawings on the foreign credits, which were extended, have been limited because it has been necessary to build up our exchange reserves to levels which will give us greater independence of action in the uncertain days which lie ahead of us.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the light of our export position and our over-all balance of payments position, are my hon. friends really prepared to maintain that the present official quotation of the Canadian dollar is not realistic? These factors would seem to me to lead to the conclusion, if anything, that the present exchange rate of our currency is too low, and that the Canadian dollar should be appreciated. I know that some of my hon. friends opposite will say that the favourable results we achieved in our trading position in 1948 were partly due to the special grants and loans given to some of our European customers by the United States government under the European recovery plan, and that had it not been for these grants to Europe the picture might have been quite different so far as our exports are concerned. Let me say here, Mr. Speaker, that in my opinion the action taken by the United States government in initiating the European recovery program last April represents one of the most statesmanlike and farsighted actions of national policy that the world has ever seen. I think it is fair to say that the future history of the civilized world, which includes Canadian history, might well have been quite different if our great and strong neighbour had not decided to lend this further and magnificent 29087-99a
Foreign Exchange Control assistance to the recovery of the western world.
The exact impact of that assistance on Canada in 1948 is not directly ascertainable, as one can only guess what would have happened to our exports in the absence of this special financing of Europe by the ECA. However, for purposes of the question which I am discussing, let us take it for granted that the availability of ECA funds was an important factor in enabling western European countries to maintain their purchases in Canada in 1948. I accept it. Well, what inferences can and should one draw from that assumption? Should the house draw the inference that the Canadian dollar is not quoted at a realistic level? Well, such an inference, it seems to me, would surely be unwarranted. After all, there is nothing in the ECA legislation which forces recipients of this financial assistance to spend their money in Canada. They spend money in Canada because they get good value for their money here, which means that at the prevailing rate of exchange for the Canadian dollar they get at least as much for their money in Canada as they do anywhere else. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we are able to compete in world markets. And if there is any better definition than that of a realistic rate of exchange I hope that before this debate is over one of my hon. friends opposite will give me that definition.
Perhaps the inference some of my hon. friends want the house to draw from the fact that our European customers are financing part of their purchases in Canada with ECA funds is that world trade rests on unstable and uncertain foundations. If that is their inference I heartily agree with them, but I cannot agree with them if they draw from that the conclusion that we should devalue the Canadian dollar. I ask them in what way they think that it is going to restore balance to the dollar account of the United Kingdom and other war-damaged countries, and help them to maintain their purchases in Canada by taking such action. These countries are in need of special dollar assistance for the obvious reason that they are not able to obtain enough dollars through exports of goods and services to meet their dollar requirements. Notwithstanding the special financial assistance given to them through ECA, they have cut down on their imports from dollar countries in an attempt to balance their account. Canadian exports have of course been affected by these restrictions, and the government is greatly concerned with the problem and is seeking, in conjunction with other countries, for an alleviation of the situation; but the Canadian exporters who are affected by this situation will, I know,

Foreign Exchange Control agree with me when I say that their difficulties do not arise because their prices are too high -a situation which might be corrected of course by a change in the exchange rate- but because the foreign countries simply will not make dollars available for certain goods; and the lowering of the Canadian exchange rate could do nothing to correct that situation. On the contrary it would aggravate it.
The trouble of course lies, as I have said, in the inability in present circumstances of the United Kingdom and certain other overseas countries to earn enough dollars to pay for the goods we would like to ship to them and they would like to have from us. A depreciation of the Canadian dollar would make it more difficult for them to earn dollars here to spend on our exports, and a moment's reflection will show the accuracy of that statement. One would think that it would be pretty obvious, but it does not seem as clear as it should be to some people.
I was struck by the statement made by the leader of the opposition at a press conference a week or so ago when he was quoted as saying that the Canadian dollar should be devalued to a realistic level. Then he went on to say this, according to the newspaper quotation:
. . . primarily today on the necessity of increasing British imports to this country as a means of maintaining our overseas trade.
That is a most desirable thing to do, but the action which my hon. friend appeared to be advocating would have exactly the opposite effect, and I hope that when he speaks he will explain to the house and to the country just how the depreciation of the Canadian dollar by say 10 per cent would help the export of British goods to Canada. It would have this effect: a British manufactured article which costs now $100 would then cost $110. Does he suggest that that increase in terms of Canadian dollars would help the United Kingdom to sell more in this market? One of the main reasons why they are unable to sell as much as they wish to is that their costs are now too high, and they find it difficult to compete with domestic prices. Of course it is true that devaluation or depreciation, which has been suggested, would result in the price of United States imports increasing. But who, under present conditions, does the house think is in a better competitive position to cope with the increased Canadian dollar cost of imports that would result from the depreciation of our dollar-the British exporter who is already finding difficulty in competing here at the prevailing exchange rate, or the United States exporter?
I hope I have said enough to make it clear that depreciation of the Canadian dollar is,


in the opinion of the Canadian government, no answer at all to the difficult world trade situation which is developing. It is no answer because it does not strike at the root of the trouble which is, I repeat, the difficulty experienced by the United Kingdom and other overseas countries in exporting enough goods to pay for their purchases in this country; and far from helping the situation the action some hon. members opposite appear to have in their mind would, as I have said before, aggravate it and worsen the lot of these exporters.
I think I have demonstrated conclusively that if you apply the normal tests of competitive capacity, that is ability to compete on the world market and ability to produce an equilibrium in our international payments, the present exchange rate is, to say the least, realistic. Some people may say: "Very well, but you are not saying anything about capital movements." I am going to deal with the question now. I will deal with it not because I really believe that our exchange rate on the dollar should be determined by considerations relating to capital movement, but because 1 want to analyse all that there may be in the case put forward by some of my hon. friends, and particularly the hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram). The case they try to make, as I understand it, is that up to the time the government took the decision to appreciate the Canadian dollar in July, 1946, there was a considerable inflow of capital from the United States and that this inflow came abruptly to an end when parity of exchange with the United States dollar was established in July of that year. In other words, it is said that the American investors were willing to put their money in Canada only if they were able to buy the necessary dollars at a 10 per cent discount, but not if they had to pay par, presumably because they regarded par as an unrealistic rate. And that argument is further developed, that the cessation of capital inflow deprived Canadian industry of a much-needed source of venture capital which would help develop the economic resources of the country. No American capitalist, the argument runs, would be sufficiently misguided to put money into a country foolish enough to try to maintain an artificial exchange rate by means of a system of exchange control. I hope my hon. friends will agree that that is a fair statement of the argument that is made. If they do not, then I should be only too glad to quote from statements of those who are like-minded, made along similar lines, but in much less temperate language.
Now, let us look at the facts. One fact is that there has, in recent years, been a decline in net American purchases of outstanding

Canadian securities. I emphasize the word "outstanding." This is the only fact that my hon. friends opposite appear to see. A second fact is that in 1944, 1945 and the first half of 1946-that is, before the change in exchange rate-the great bulk of Canadian securities purchased by American investors consisted of dominion, provincial and municipal government bonds. In the period mentioned, net sales to American investors of securities in these classifications amounted to $275 million or 72 per cent of the total. A third fact is that the decline which occurred in net American purchases of outstanding securities in recent years has been much more important in the case of government securities than in the case of industrial securities.
What is the significance of these three facts? Even if one assumes that the decline in American buying of outstanding securities was largely influenced by the change in the exchange rate rather than by the reduction which occurred in the public offerings of government of Canada securities, or by other causes, the main significance of the decline is that this indirect form of government borrowing in the United States came to an end.
Well, to take the words which my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) used yesterday-"So what?" Does anyone opposite actually think the government should offer its securities to American investors at cut rates, for 90-cent dollars? Is it not more advantageous if the government wishes to borrow in the United States, for it to borrow directly as we did when we put out the $150 million in the New York market, the fifteen-year issue of last summer at 3 per cent-and the terms, incidentally, which are much better for the government and for the people of Canada than those involved in the other indirect type of borrowing to which I have referred, terms which could not be bettered by any other country in the world.
It is quite likely that the restoration of the Canadian dollar to parity did cause certain American investors, who had bought Cana-dian-dollar security in the belief that the Canadian dollar was bound to go back to par, to reduce their purchases and in some cases liquidate their holdings and take profits. They had indeed made the speculative profit which they had anticipated.
What conclusions should one draw from this regarding the proper exchange rate policy for Canada? I put this question: Should we maintain a continuously undervalued exchange rate so that American investors who wish to take a position here will at all times expect that the value of the Canadian dollar is going to be increased?
Foreign Exchange Control If you keep this up long enough the Canadian dollar will not have any value at all. It will disappear altogether.
I hardly think my hon. friends can be recommending that course. But it is precisely these anticipations regarding future changes in the exchange rate which seem to play an important part in determining the attitudes of some non-resident investors toward outstanding Canadian securities.
In this connection it should be noted that, during a large part of the time which has elapsed between January 1946 and the present time, American investors who wished to purchase Canadian domestic securities have been able to get the Canadian dollars through the unofficial market at about the same 10 per cent discount as prevailed before the exchange rate was changed.
I have stressed the fact that the bulk of the net American purchases of outstanding Canadian securities, when this type of capital inflow was at its height, consisted in the purchase of government securities, and that the great bulk of the decline in net American purchases which has occurred in recent years has been concentrated in that particular class of security.
From this fact we are invited to draw the conclusion that there has been no real increase in American investment in Canada in recent years. And that is simply not true. The real investment of American capital in Canadian industry has gone on increasing year by year. I am not referring now to the purchase of outstanding securities but to the bricks and mortar type of investment in which the non-resident investor brings skill and know-how and makes a direct contribution to the development of the economic resources of the country.

I have not those figures here, but I have no doubt they are available. I shall take note of the hon. member's point and see that they are made available to him. The great bulk of it, as I said a moment ago, was in the purchase of outstanding Canadian government securities, whether dominion, provincial or municipal. The great bulk of investment immediately prior to the war was in that type of security, and not so much in the industrial type of security.
Perhaps I have said enough now about the capital movements aspect of our international transactions to refute the notion that this reflects the maintenance of an unrealistic exchange rate. We do not need to offer the Canadian dollar at bargain-basement prices to attract desirable capital investment to this country. It is quite possible that we might be able to attract some speculative in-and-out investments by doing so, but I can assure you that this government is not going to base its exchange policy upon that type of Canadian investment.
There is one other reason, as invalid as the rest, which is sometimes given for considering the present exchange rate as unrealistic. That is the existence of this so-called unofficial market for Canadian dollars in New York in which the Canadian dollar is currently quoted at a discount of 6| to 7 per cent. In the press conference to which I have already referred, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) apparently indicated that the unofficial market rate was the yardstick which in his judgment could be taken in determining where exchange should be pegged. From that, I gather he thinks that represents a realistic quotation of the Canadian dollar.

I should like to look at that proposal for a moment. First, no resident of Canada ever has occasion to acquire foreign exchange through the unofficial market at the discount prevailing there. All the foreign exchange bought by Canadians is bought at official rates. Foreigners receiving payment in Canadian dollars from Canadians in payment of imports, in payment of current services of all types, in payment of interest and dividends, in payment of freights and the like, can convert these Canadian dollars into foreign exchange at the official rates of exchange. There are, however, a few types of payments to non-residents, representing capital items, which we are not prepared to convert into foreign exchange at the official rates. For example, an American holding a security maturing in Canada can, and does, receive the face value of that security payable in Canadian dollars, and he will come into Canadian dollars as a result of the maturity of that security which we are not prepared to provide exchange for out of our official reserves. The various types of payment of this kind and their magnitude are described in detail in the report of the foreign exchange control board. I shall not weary the house by reviewing them here, but non-residents who come into possession of Canadian dollars which they are hot able to convert into United States dollars at the official rate may have some use for them in Canada; for instance, they may purchase another security here. If they have not, they are free to sell them to some other non-resident, to some other American, who may have some use for the dollars, at a price which is determined between them. It is transactions of that type whmh take place in the unofficial market.
Since the Canadian dollars acquired there are limited in the uses to which they can be put in Canada, being restricted, broadly speaking, to investment and tourist expenditures, the quotation need not be the same as the official rate. But to say that this narrow, restricted market, this market for a dollar which is only good for a few relatively unimportant purposes, gives a more realistic appraisal of the value of the Canadian dollar is, in my judgment, pure fantasy. I am prepared to leave it to the house and to the country to form their own judgment as to what constitutes the more representative and realistic rate, the rate at which Canadians were able in 1948 to obtain foreign exchange to pay for $2,600 million worth of imports, $275 million worth of freight and shipping charges, over $400 million worth of other current expenditures abroad, and at which non-resident investors were able to obtain foreign exchange in the amount of $325 million for income earned in Canada, a total of

some $3,600 million, or the rate at which a few non-residents transferred to other nonresidents some scores of millions of Canadian dollars. I am prepared to leave it to the judgment of the house and the country as to which is the more realistic rate.
I have come to the end of what I have to say about exchange rates. I have tried to examine, as carefully as I could, all the grounds which I have seen put forward for dissatisfaction with the present rates, and in the present circumstances I can And no basis for believing that the present rate is unrealistic or that it should be altered. The Canadian dollar was appreciated in 1946 very largely because we saw a marked increase in prices originating in the United States. It was realized that Canada would inevitably be affected by this, but we did not want to add to the cost of our imports, with pervasive effects throughout the whole cost of living and the cost of doing business, a further ten per cent which could be avoided through changing the exchange rate. The price developments which have taken place since 1946 have shown how well founded our expectations were, and have provided the most complete justification for the action which we took. If any hon. member believes that the cost of living in this country is too low, I hope he will get up and say so. The government, at any rate, is not prepared to add to that cost of living and the cost of doing business by depreciating the Canadian dollar.
Perhaps I can bring that issue home to every hon. member of the house, and to every household in this country, if I put it in these terms. The government sees no justification for and is not prepared to recommend an action at this time which would have the effect of imposing an additional 10 per cent tariff, or even a 7 per cent tariff, against the importation of any and all goods from any and all countries. That is what would be the effect of restoring the Canadian dollar to the wartime 90 cent basis or, alternatively, fixing it at the rate which has recently prevailed in the unofficial market. Let those who argue for the devaluation or depreciation of the Canadian dollar be frank in explaining to the Canadian people just what it will mean to their cost of living and their cost of doing business.
The moral, Mr. Speaker, of all that I have said is that there is no real alternative to the action which is now recommended to the house. I look on this as, in a sense, a measure of national defence. In the face of all the uncertainties now surrounding international trade, this country cannot afford to give up the economic defences which foreign exchange control provides because, as I have said on other occasions, a nation which loses its
Foreign Exchange Control exchange reserves loses its independence. More than ever we need to ensure, in the words of the preamble to the Foreign Exchange Control Act, that Canada's foreign exchange resources are made available to meet the needs of Canada as a whole, that they are used to promote trade and other normal cur- _ rent transactions with other countries, and not dissipated through disadvantageous exports of capital from Canada, or for other purposes disadvantageous to Canada as a whole.
Two years from now, Mr. Speaker, parliament will again have an opportunity of reviewing the situation and determining whether, in its wisdom and in the light of the then existing circumstances, it is still necessary to continue exchange control to protect the public interest.

The situation in western Europe has awakened our people. They know now that the danger is a very serious one. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) knows it is serious. Last December he said so to the people in London, and I should like to quote two or three sentences from what he said. This appeared in the Montreal Star on December 17, 1948.
Hon. J. G. Gardiner, Canada's agriculture minister, said today that Canada's hopes of long-term, large-scale food agreements with the United Kingdom were "dashed to the ground" by currency difficulties.
The minister continued:
I am convinced that the world is not in any state of mind where it can be expected to agree that the manipulation of any system or systems of currency is going to be allowed to interfere with the will of those who have empty stomachs when it is preventing their purchasing surpluses of food and distributing them.


Later, he said:
There is no plan for exchange of British cars or steel products for Canadian food although Britain gives Russia tinplate for fish.
Although Canadian production was increased largely during the war when Britain was in urgent need, British negotiators now propose imports from Canada similar to those of pre-war days.
It might be a good thing for everybody if they would close down united nations meetings long enough to permit some of the United Kingdom and the United States experts to get together and settle some basis on which dollars and sterling can be converted to allow nations like Canada to produce food to feed the starving millions and distribute it.
The Minister of Agriculture is a practical man; he knows that these difficulties exist.
What is the situation in western Europe? We all know what it is. Our trade is shrinking to the point where it is dubious whether we are going to be able to sell any of our agricultural products. Do not let anyone imagine that even the most miraculous discoveries of oil in Alberta or equally miraculous discoveries of ore in Labrador are going to solve our problem, even if they were so miraculous that they solved the payment problem in the United States. Nevertheless, unless this problem of exporting our food products to Europe is solved, you will have an economic revolution on your hands because you would have the western provinces with three or four times too many people growing food. So far as I know, the Minister of Finance made no reference to that. The Minister of Agriculture knows about it. Why would he not? He is a farmer.
What is the story in Britain? We know the story. In Britain and in western Europe you have this ironical situation. North America is sending them aid in a manner that has never before been equalled by any nation in peacetime in the economic field. What are they doing? How are they using these materials? I am not exactly blaming them, I am blaming the situation; but they are using them in order to make themselves better able to cease trading with us. Let me read briefly two extracts from the New York Times. The first article is dated February 6 and it indicates the fantastic-no other word will describe it-situation which has arisen in Europe by perpetuating the principle in this act which we are asked to renew. The government are not taking cognizance of it. They are not taking steps to meet it. They are just permitting things to roll along, and they are not rolling very well. This article is headed, "Exchange Deals hit U.S. Industry." The text reads as follows:
"Bargain currency deals" and indirect transshipment of merchandise are creating major inflationary problems for American industries which depend upon several important raw material imports, according to authoritative trade quarters here.
Then, later, it says this:
Traders and importers cited the unrealistic "official" exchange rates for certain foreign currencies, including the British pound sterling, as being chiefly to blame for the conditions which have arisen.
At this point, let me say that when we think about exchange rates we should not think only in terms of the United States dollar and the Canadian dollar. There are many other exchanges that affect this country. It seems to me the minister had very little to say about them.

One
of the results of this is that Britain is beginning to price itself out of our markets. That is coming more rapidly than we like to think. You have also another fantastic situation which is in great danger of arising, where the sterling area will deal with other countries in the sterling area on a level of prices above the rest of the world. That is something which is, as I say, making the thing fantastic. I should like to read a short extract from the last report of the chairman of the foreign exchange control board, in which he refers to this sterling situation. I read from page 5:
The prices at which commodities are exchanged in such bilateral deals are frequently considerably higher than those prevailing for similar goods outside the protected trading area. Moreover, the discriminatory restrictions imposed on dollar expenditures keep out competition from the western hemisphere while the special financial arrangements referred to encourage trade within the area. I again ask this question. Facing the situation that the governor of the bank describes there, have we anything to offer? Has the government nothing to say to us except to ask us again to continue the paralysing influence of this act that was passed two years ago? Surely it is fair to say that we have now a new situation. I mean, it is a new situation by reason of the fact that we are faced with this grave dislocation of our trade with western Europe. Some people will say -with a certain amount of truth-and I come now to the question that was asked a few minutes ago-that this dislocation exists because trade has got all snarled up, because we have not been able to reach multilateral trade as we had hoped, and that we have other difficulties. In a measure that is true. On the other hand, I think it is equally true to say that one of the things holding back trade is this matter of unreal exchanges. One of the things that give me hope is that inside the sterling area they are beginning to find that out. I think it is a case of action and reaction. I would suggest that our action is hurting us in two ways. First of all it is hurting us with regard to European trade.
Next I want to take up a point that the Minister of Finance made. He pooh-poohed the idea that we are suffering anything by reason of the loss of American investment. I am aware of what he says, namely, that money is coming up here for bricks and mortar. As I understand it, they do a kind of complicated deal with the foreign exchange control board. If you are an American wanting to come up here to invest, apparently you go in a humble manner to the board and say, I want to spend $5 million, let us say. Then you make a deal, and the board says: If you will buy $2,500,000 at our rate, then we will allow you to buy $2,500,000 at the so-called free rate or whatever you wish to call it. In other words, the board recognizes that rate in an extremely real manner. Although the minister laughed at it and pooh-poohed it, nevertheless his creature, his own board, recognizes that rate, and a great many of the transactions take place under it.
Now I want to deal with what the minister said. He rather sneered at people who merely want to invest money. He prefers bricks and mortar to money. In a way I do also. But let us remember this fact. Ever since the year 1608 this country has been in need of outside investment. We have always needed outside investment. Anyone who does not face that situation is just not looking at the facts.

The second thing I wish to point out is that as long as we have this situation where people put their money in and have it impounded, then we shall have a brake on investment. Although the minister did not say it-he may believe it but he certainly abstained from saying it-what we should aim at as our objective is to get back to the situation we had in the past where people could bring money here and take it out. It was a most useful cushion in the 1920's. It has been a useful cushion again and again to have Americans ready to come in here and invest their money. That we are not suffering now is possible merely because for the moment we have continuing huge government expenditure, high employment and so on. The time will likely come-and it may be nearer than anyone wants to think-when we shall want all the American investment we can get, and it will be available if we are strong enough to get to the situation where we can do away with these rigid exchanges. I am not going to suggest that it be done tonight, but I have a suggestion nevertheless.
There is another thing we should bear in mind. I am sure the minister has not enjoyed the comments that have been made from time to time with regard to him as the author of austerity. Having been brought up as a Presbyterian I am a great believer in austerity, but I think it should take more convenient forms.

At the present time the only right we have, if we want to change the value of the dollar, is to say that we will make it ninety-five cents or ninety-three cents or whatever you like. Why should not there be a range within which it might swing? Why should we not call on Bretton Woods or the international monetary fund and say, they can change the agreement; the agreement can be changed. Why should we not have an arrangement of flexibility whereby the government might say, we are going to support the dollar at ninety cents? We shall let it swing from where it is to ninety cents. Incidentally, if the fund took that forward step, it seems to me that it might encourage other countries to come forward and try to make at least a beginning, instead of this barren resolution which just says, let us go on for two years more as we are, and have everything getting worse and worse.

We should try very hard not only to get our own exchange rate realistic, but what is just as important, other people's as well, because exchange rates work two ways. This thing need not be as hopeless as the minister suggests by shaking his head, by which he means that we cannot do anything about it. I believe we can do something about it. The thing is not as hopeless as all that. The Americans are being utterly realistic about this in the economic co-operation act under which they are making the advances we know of which are without precedent in the history of the world, as the London Economist pointed out, without precedent in peacetime in the history of the world. Nevertheless they are realistic, and they have the right-and I should think it is a right which they will avail themselves of-to ask people who are participating in the benefits of their fund to come and discuss their exchange rates with the international monetary fund. What does that mean? I think that the Americans who, as I say, are keeping western Europe going, are going to be realistic about this. They are not going to let this thing go on to the point where after three or four years, all that they succeed in doing is to set up a situation which makes it impossible for them to trade with the sterling area. I say that the Americans have the right to do that. The international monetary fund is the medium which they

Foreign Exchange Control have chosen for this. They reserve to themselves the right to call in the beneficiary nations to discuss it in that way.
I have tried to outline what I think should be done. We in this party are not going to accept this resolution as is. We are not going to vote for this foreign exchange act as is, which has the effect of continuing the present rigidity. We believe that the time has come when our government and other governments as well-we can only speak for ourselves-should take steps to move toward realism, and therefore I move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mr. Casselman):

1.	The Canadian dollar should be allowed to seek its true economic level within the limits imposed by the Bretton Woods agreement; and
2.	It is expedient to present a measure to provide for the continuance in force of foreign exchange control with necessary modifications for not more than one year to permit representations to be made to the international monetary fund with a view to obtaining such modifications in its regulations as will permit an orderly revaluation of currencies to bring them to realistic levels and thus make the further continuation of foreign exchange control unnecessary.

I should like to say something about the measure now before us. This is a very important one, from the point of view of Canada's economy. As has been said by both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), Canada's economic situation is vulnerable when viewed in the light of world conditions at the present time; and any government or parliament which fails to protect our country in the present circumstances is in my opinion derelict in its duty.
Consequently I believe the attention of the house should be directed to the resolution, and the proposals lying behind it. May I say to my hon. friends of the government and of the official opposition that there is one thing which people everywhere are coming more and more to realize, and that is that unrestricted private or free enterprise is no longer a policy any government can follow. More and more, by the circumstances and the evolution of history and society, governments are forced more and more to protect their people and to direct the economy of their various countries. That is particularly true I believe in the international field at the present time.
I have noticed that again and again hon. gentlemen who have objected to control measures before the house in the past few days have risen in their places when the orders of the day have been called and asked the government to do this or that to protect various parts of our economy, and various interests in that economy. More and more we are going to be driven to the point where governments have to give attention to the

economic relationships in the domestic field as well as our economic relationships with other nations of the world.
To say that the emergency following the war has passed is, I suggest, particularly unrealistic. We have only to look around the world today to realize that in almost every field of human endeavour, in almost every one of our relationships, emergencies exist. And in this House of Commons, ever since we met on January 26, day by day some phase of one or other of these emergencies has been brought to the attention of the house by individual private members and by the government itself-and by the official opposition as well, incidentally.
Consequently a measure of this description which has a tremendous bearing upon our economic relationships with other countries must receive the consideration of parliament at this time. And whether we agree with all the implications of this policy, whether we agree or not with the manner in which it has been operated, the fundamental principle behind the proposal must be endorsed and accepted by the House of Commons, if we are to protect our economy in the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time.
