The house resumed consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to provide for the continuance in force of the Foreign Exchange Control Act until sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament commencing in the year 1951.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying before the supper hour that I thought that any government must take steps to protect the economy of this country in the face of the difficulties which now confront the world, and bearing in mind particularly that the Canadian situation has been made more difficult because of the historic pattern of our trade in the past. For years we were in the very happy position in normal times of being able to sell almost everything that we wished to sell to the United Kingdom and western Europe, and with the dollars we earned we were able to buy in the United States almost everything that we wished to buy. The result was that this triangular trade benefited Canada considerably in the past, but today it makes our situation peculiarly difficult.
Great Britain and the western European countries, the Netherlands, Belgium, and other nations, have lost much of the income they once received from overseas. That, of course, is more particularly true of Great Britain, who liquidated so many of her over-

seas investments in order to meet the obligations of our common war. It is quite true that over the past year and a half the exchange situation has greatly improved as far as Canada is concerned. I think, however, that to some extent that is an improvement at the expense of our own Canadian people, and that we should be wary lest our people suffer further. What I have in mind is that because of the restrictions that the government imposed in regard to imports from the United States, and because the government insisted we were under obligation, because of the Geneva agreement although some of us did not agree with that point of view, to. exercise non-discrimination, we had to put the same impediments against the inflow of goods from the United Kingdom and other countries as we did upon those from the United States.
Then, too, as soon as the war ended there was a great deal of pressure for protection by certain Canadian manufacturers. At any rate, the government removed some of the advantages that Great Britain had enjoyed during the war by reimposing certain tariffs that were in the interests of the textile industry, the glass industry, and other industries in our country that had arisen behind policies in the nature of protective tariffs. To my mind, the continuance of such policies will be serious for the farmers of Canada, because after all we can produce vast quantities of food in Canada, and unless we can find permanent markets for the great surpluses we produce, surpluses which would be surpluses even if our own people were fed adequately, then agriculture in this country faces a very difficult future indeed.
Therefore I say to the government that, while we believe that the exercise of control over foreign exchange is essential at this time, nevertheless we believe that there are other factors which the government should take into consideration in dealing with these problems. We have increased our exports to the United States, but I think that most people will agree that the United States market for Canadian goods has always been a very uncertain one. There have been times when they were prepared to take quantities of certain classes of goods from us, and then from time to time, when they found that they could themselves produce the goods that they were taking from us, we lost those markets. We have seen these fluctuations ever since I have been in the country, now some forty years.
Then there is also the peculiar situation in the United States that no one seems to know what is going to happen internally to their economy. Like our own economy, it is buoyed

up at the moment by these tremendous expenditures, we will call them, though in reality they are exports of tremendous quantities of goods abroad, thus maintaining a very high level of employment in that country. Lately, however, we have seen a somewhat sharp drop in certain prices in the United States. There is considerable unemployment and we have seen certain classes of farm commodities drop in price. In our own country we have had similar and quite spectacular drops. I mentioned the other day that on the speculative market a year or so ago rye was selling for around $4, but when I looked at the paper the other night I saw that it was down to below $1.20. It is the same thing with barley; it has fluctuated widely. Where you have the kind of economy that is subject to great fluctuations there is grave danger. That will be particularly the case if we are tied up completely to the United States. Therefore I think that, while the increase in our exports to the United States, and the lowering of our imports from the United States, have improved our dollar position, nevertheless there are dangers in connection with what has occurred during the past year or so. I say therefore that we have to look to the principal customers whom we have had in the past.
I noted this afternoon the criticism that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) made of the British trading so largely in the sterling area, entering into bilateral agreements, and so on. We have to bear in mind that what they are actually doing is what we should be doing. They are more or less digging into the markets which were their natural, reliable and normal markets before the war. They are endeavouring to protect themselves in that regard as well as to prevent the loss of those dollars which they need badly in the dollar area, and of which they are short at the present time. Indeed, while we may take steps of the description of those that are now being considered under this foreign exchange control measure, it seems to me that the final solution of our problems, as well as of the problems of the world, lies more and more in co-operation on the widest possible basis, and with the largest possible group of nations across the world.
At the moment I confess that I cannot see any immediate hope for a return to wider trade relationships than we know now. We see all of the European countries endeavouring to rebuild their own economies, to produce more and more goods for export, and unless we in our country can receive more and more of the goods that they can export, then we cannot export goods to them. I want
Foreign Exchange Control to emphasize again that the old pattern of trade, which benefited Canada so greatly, has disappeared. Our overseas customers, and particularly the United Kingdom with her vast overseas investments, had a steady flow of goods under that pattern of trade, which brought in the dollars with which she could make payment to us from time to time; and those dollars have disappeared because the investments which gave rise to them have disappeared as far as the British are concerned.
It strikes me that what the British are actually doing at the present time is endeavouring to protect themselves in the future against a further loss of trade, and to build up in their island, with their great population, an export trade that will enable them to obtain the raw materials and the foodstuffs that are vital to the existence of their country.
While we may be critical of some of the things they have done because they may react against our own country at the moment, I think it is understandable why they are doing them. The point I am making is that we should endeavour to be realistic, too, where tariff barriers or trade barriers of any description prevent goods coming into our country from overseas that could be used to buy goods here which we could export and must export if we are to remain prosperous, because we produce them in quantities too great to be used within our own country. So I say we have to consider more than both the exchange and other factors in the situation.
This afternoon I heard the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) suggest that we should let the dollar find its own level. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) answered that previously when he asked what is that level. If we take the market referred to as the free market, that level is not very much below the rate at which the foreign exchange control board exchanges our currency for that of the United States. But it seems to me that with a fluctuating Canadian dollar, a dollar that might be depreciated- 1 think it was suggested last session that we should allow the Canadian dollar to depreciate as much as thirty per cent-if the Canadian dollar depreciated ten per cent the cost of living for the mass of the people of this country would probably increase by more than ten per cent. We are so dependent upon the United States for many of our raw materials and many foodstuffs; and anything which tends to depreciate our dollar means that we must find more Canadian funds with which to purchase United States currency in order to buy American goods, and the cost of living here would increase proportionately. Consequently I believe that suggestion would benefit relatively few people in this country.

Foreign Exchange Control I am free to admit that it might benefit certain speculative interests. It might benefit some of the gold-mining interests in the country, though I would point out that already the government has made considerable concessions to that industry in order to assist it. So, since the depreciation of our dollar would be done only at the expense of sacrificing our agriculture. and the standard of living of our people, I think the suggestion is thoroughly unsound and I would oppose it on those grounds. We remember very well that back in the twenties there were considerable investments in our country coming from the United States, but when things got a bit tough not only did the banks in our own country withdraw loans but there was some flight of United States capital as well. I would not be inclined to suggest to the minister or to the government that they should follow the example of what was done in the twenties. We must bear in mind that the twenties were followed by the thirties, and we all remember what happened at that time, when we allowed our own dollar to remain tied to the gold standard and how that affected primary producers all over this country.
I do not propose to prolong this discussion, Mr. Speaker, because I think the principal debate should be on second reading of the bill, when we know exactly what is before us. I did want to say, however, that I believe no government in any country, in the circumstances now existing all over the world, can do other than exercise a considerable amount of economic control in order to protect its own nationals, its own domestic economy and indeed its international trade. That, I take it, is the purpose of the resolution before us at the present time; and because we believe that to be the purpose we are going to support it when the vote is taken.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I find myself pretty well in agreement with the stand taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the question of exchange and the valuation of the dollar. I think the price level in Canada compares very favourably with the price levels in other countries. I would say to the minister, however, that if a situation develops such as we had in the thirties, when the prices of agricultural products fell to a low level and we had great difficulty competing with other countries whose currency was depreciated considerably below the dollar, then the primary producers of this country would be justified in demanding that the dollar be depreciated also. That situation has not
arisen, however, and we hope it does not recur. On the other hand, if the government were prepared to stabilize the prices of agricultural products, then of course agriculture would no longer be concerned with the level at which the dollar might be maintained on the international market.
The international situation today I think demonstrates the need for continuation of the foreign exchange control board. On the one hand there is the ever-present danger of an adverse balance of payments with the United States. On the other hand there is the danger of losing essential markets in Europe owing to the shortage of dollars. I am going to confine my remarks mainly to the second of these points. I notice the measure is intended to continue the board for only two years. I am satisfied that it will be necessary to continue the operations of the foreign exchange control board for a far longer period than that. Both the problems I mentioned are being aggravated at the present time, I think, by the operation of the Bret-ton Woods agreement and the non-discrimination clauses in the Geneva trade agreement. That trade agreement has not passed this house, but I understand the government has signed it and that we are actually operating under it. On several occasions I have explained why we are opposed to certain policies under the Bretton Woods agreement, so I am not going to take any time to deal with that matter this evening except to mention it later on in regard to one or two other matters. However, today we are operating under those agreements whether we like them or not, and certainly as long as we continue to do so there will be a very real need for continuation of the operation of the foreign exchange control board. Even if those agreements were replaced by others which would operate for the benefit and advantage of all trading nations, I am convinced there would still be a need for a foreign exchange control board, though no doubt in that case controls would be exercised mainly for the purpose of trading to the greatest extent possible with those nations which would balance their trade with us.
This does not mean for one moment that we in this group endorse everything that has been done by the foreign exchange control board. Many things have been brought to my attention that have seemed indefensible, though I quite realize that if those matters were investigated it might be found that while they appeared inadvisable there were grounds that really justified the action taken by the board. I have had several matters referred to me which I have taken up with the board.

On each occasion I was given every consideration, as was the question I raised.
Both the problems I have mentioned, that is the adverse balance of trade with the United States and the shrinking of our markets in Europe, are the logical outcome of certain policies carried out under the Bretton Woods agreement. I say that because so long as the exporting nations have the right to demand payment in their own currency instead of accepting the goods of other nations in return, I think there is bound to be trouble. In fact, I would say that as long as that situation exists we will have trouble in maintaining a balance of trade with European countries. That is what is happening today. True, our trade surplus with Europe is today apparently being reduced, but not so much by an increase in imports from those countries as by a reduction in exports from Canada to them.
The 1948 report of the foreign exchange control board makes this quite clear. At the bottom of page 14 of that report it is stated:
However, If allowance is made for the rise in both export and import prices in 1948 it is apparent that though there was an appreciable rise in the volume of imports into Canada from these countries the contraction in the volume of our exports was the more important factor in reducing our trade surplus.
In the middle of the next page it is stated:
Nearly every appreciable decrease in our exports to sterling area and other ERP countries can be traced to a change in import policy on the part of the foreign government concerned.
I point out that if nations were unable to obtain dollars with which to buy our goods, in order to avoid a greater deficit they were forced to reduce imports from this country. They had no other alternative. It is also interesting to note that that action was advised by the international monetary fund. In the report of the fund for 1948, on page 12, I find that European nations were advised that they should reduce their imports from the western area and try to increase their imports from Asia and Africa. Referring to Asia and Africa, the report says this:
These areas might also be further developed as alternative sources for certain European imports and this would diminish European demands for imports from the western hemisphere.
I have heard some people become quite critical regarding Britain's action in buying from other nations instead of buying from Canada. In fact, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) seemed to be rather critical. Britain, however, has no alternative if we demand payment in dollars. Britain has not got the dollars and we will not supply her with the dollars because we have curtailed our imports from that country. As long as
Foreign Exchange Control we continue a policy of that kind we are forcing Britain to trade elsewhere because she has not the dollars to trade with us.

speechtext:
The report of the foreign exchange control board expresses regret that a greater balance was not restored by increased exports from Europe to Canada. At the bottom of page 15 the report states:
There is, therefore, reason for some concern that these countries did not export more to us, particularly in view of the fact that the net effect of the government of Canada's import restrictions enforced during 1948 was to encourage imports from overseas countries. Notwithstanding the improvement noted, only eighteen per cent of our imports came from the United Kingdom and other sterling area countries in 1948, compared to twenty-nine per cent before the war.
It is all very well to express regret that Europe did not export more goods to us, but two countries are involved. Europe cannot export more goods to us unless we are prepared to buy them.
I noticed that Mr. W. G. Coventry, the British trade commissioner, speaking before the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at Saskatoon, stated that there would be a permanent market for a large volume of surplus Canadian farm products in the United Kingdom when British exports to Canada reach $500 million annually. It was for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that we opposed the Bretton Woods agreement. At that time, we prophesied that a policy of that kind with regard to our exports of Europe would be bound to fail because those countries would not be in a position to pay for them with dollars.
I should like to refer to a statement in the report of the foreign exchange control board which I think puts this whole problem in a nutshell. First, of all, I should like to quote this statement, then briefly analyse it. It is to be found on pages 6 and 7 and I will read first from page 6:
If efforts on the part of the sterling area and ERP countries in the direction of greater exports to dollar countries are inadequate or fail to solve their dollar problem, then it may be expected that these countries will continue to place special restrictions on imports from dollar countries. The countries whose exports are affected by these restrictions will be confronted with the choice of finding some alternative use, at home or in other foreign markets, for the goods previously exported to the dollar-short countries or making special arrangements in an effort to retain these markets. These arrangements could involve the provision of the exports without payment in foreign exchange, through the extension of grants or credits, or special deals in which the exporting country agreed to use the proceeds of its exports to take more goods from its dollar-short customers even though these goods were higher in price than had to be paid elsewhere. To ir ake room

Foreign Exchange Control for these relatively high-priced imports it would be necessary to impose discriminatory import restrictions.
I wish to deal with two or three of the alternatives given in that statement. The statement is made that:
The countries whose exports are affected by these restrictions will be confronted with the choice of finding some alternative use, at home-
Mr. Speaker, I think that is a very important point. On most questions of trade, it is a matter of getting two countries to agree, but here is a suggestion that if we are not able to export goods we should try to find ways and means of utilizing some of these goods in the home market. It is solely within the power of this government to deal with that matter. I would suggest that many of the goods we are trying to. export today could very well be utilized in Canada. After all, we have a tremendous potential market in this country if we would only develop it. Therefore, as the first step in dealing with this problem, I would suggest that the government take action to increase the purchasing power of the people in the lower income brackets to at least the point where they can have a decent standard of living; at least, to the point where they could purchase the agricultural products we have in abundance.
I would point out that that is not only the answer to finding a market for goods we cannot export, but it would be just as important if we were able to export goods and bring back goods in return, because if we bring back goods in return for our exports the same difficulty will apply. It will be difficult for us to find markets for our imports. The international monetary fund stressed that problem on page 13 of the report:
A high level of demand in the western hemisphere will be a necessary condition for increasing exports to this region. A further relaxation of tariffs and import quotas in the western hemisphere countries applicable to primary commodities as well as to manufactured goods would be helpful in encouraging the necessary increase and redirection of world trade. But recognition of these considerations should not obscure the fact that Europe's need to increase its exports to the western hemisphere arises not only from the exceptional circumstances of the transitional period but also from more enduring changes in the world economic structure.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, we are making a grave mistake if we look upon this as a merely temporary condition. We can trace the origination of this condition back to the year 1913. It was aggravated by two wars, but even if there had been no wars we would have had to face this question in the very near future. I think the government, therefore, ought to take heed of the recommendation that was made by the federation of agriculture regarding the allocation of food.
I think the suggestion was put forward by

Professor Hope, who is the economic adviser to the federation of agriculture. I understand the proposal is an extension of the old food-stamp plan. I remember when the food-stamp plan was first introduced in the United States, whereby surplus food could be sold to people in low-income groups at a fraction of its cost. The Christian Science Monitor pointed out that it was an adaptation of Mr. Douglas' social credit idea.
I do not care what you call it. I think it would be a good way to dispose of large quantities of agricultural products that are surplus. Perhaps I might just quote Professor Hope with regard to the way this plan might operate. I quote from the Alberta wheat pool budget of February 11, 1949 as follows:
Reducing farm production during a depression simply causes scarcity of food and increases the misery of unemployed and the low income groups of consumers. Therefore the only correct and sound solution under such circumstances is to maintain or restore to a decent level consumer purchasing power for food.
This statement was made by Dr. E. C. Hope, economist with the Canadian federation of agriculture in an address to the annual convention held at Saskatoon last week.
Dr. Hope said that, should we run into a major depression, no price support program for agriculture could last if it depended merely upon withdrawing supplies from the market by a government agency. Creating artificial scarcity, he said, is just aping industry. He suggested first a large scale useful public works program to maintain employment at reasonable levels, and second, a food allotment plan similar to the one established in the United States.
Under the United States food allotment plan a family can purchase for forty per cent of its monthly income a food coupon book which will buy sufficient food each month for an adequate diet. Each month or so the government calculates how much it costs to provide an adequate diet for different sized families. If the cost is $60 for a family of four, and the declared monthly income of that family is $100, a coupon book with a food value of $60 can be purchased by that family for $40. If the family income is only $80 the book can be bought for $32. If the family income is $150 a month or over it will not pay to purchase the coupon book. The difference between the $60 value of the coupon book and the cash paid by the family for the same is provided by the federal treasury.
A program of this sort, said Dr. Hope, would mean that every family would be guaranteed an adequate diet regardless of income. In times of depression and unemployment this would increase the demand for food because the people with low incomes would be able to bid for food against the people with higher incomes.
American economists have estimated that had such a plan been in operation in the United States during the 1930's, prices for farm products would have been maintained close to ninety per cent of their calculated parity level without any other price support program.
So I suggest to the government that it might be worth while thoroughly to investigate that plan as a means to helping maintain a demand for our own production and the imports we bring into this country, because that problem is going to grow steadily as time

goes on. Once these nations that are getting on their feet are in the position not only to pay for their imports by their exports but in addition to start to pay back their loans in goods, how are we to maintain in this country markets for those goods? There is only one way, and that is by taking steps to increase purchasing power to the point where it can pay for those goods.

speechtext:
It is paid out of the federal treasury. Professor Hope does not say how it is to be financed. So long as this government is in power, it is its responsibility. I do not intend to suggest how to finance it. We have our own views as to how it should be done. Certainly it should not be done by increased taxation. If there is a lack of effective demand in the country and you are going to try to eliminate that lack of demand by increasing taxation to expand purchasing power you are going to get nowhere. The government would no doubt do it by borrowing from the chartered banks. We would suggest that it be done through the Bank of Canada. This paragraph goes on to say:
These arrangements could involve the provision of the exports without payment in foreign exchange, through the extension of grants or credits, or special deals in which the exporting country agreed to use the proceeds of its exports to take more goods . . .
Well, Mr. Speaker, it might be done as the board suggests, by making gifts to countries, but I am not advocating that, unless the country is in a state where it cannot possibly carry on without that help. It might be done by loans, but I am not suggesting that it be done in that way if that country is in a position to pay by exports of goods. I am suggesting that the logical way in which to deal with that program is this. Instead of insisting on payment in dollars, we should be willing to accept sterling from the country, that is a blocked credit. Then with that blocked credit we could buy from Britain the goods we require. That is of course a straight bilateral deal; but that could very easily be put on a multilateral basis by establishing an international exchange so that blocked credits held in one country could be traded for the blocked credits held in another. It would be multilateral trade on a goods basis instead of on a dollar basis. It is interesting to note that the London chamber of commerce of England, the members of which are not the type of crack-pots the Minister of Agriculture was talking about when he was in England, but who are a bunch of hardheaded businessmen, men who probably have
Foreign Exchange Control a greater understanding of international trade than has any other body of men in the world, are suggesting a system of that kind.
I should like to quote briefly from "A Twentieth Century Economic System", a system endorsed by the London chamber of commerce. Referring to the matter with which I have just dealt, it states:
The above is a simple example of bilateral trade, but multilateral trade could be provided for by the exchange controls of the participating nations having representatives at an international exchange where blocked credits in one country could be exchanged for those in another at the conventionally fixed exchange rates: the primary responsibility for establishing a contra account, by importing from the country to which a sale had been made, would remain with the exporting country. If it did not wish to do so that would be its affair and not that of the importing country, which would have done its part by establishing the necessary credit. The importing country would be entitled to cancel the credit, under a statute of limitations, if it were not used within seven years. The principle is that with which we are ail familiar in internal trading: if you have a credit with a shop, you cannot take it out in cash but you clear it when you take goods.
It is interesting to recall that when Professor Keynes brought forward his white paper he suggested it might be wise to institute a statute of limitations; that is to say, where nations pile up credits in other countries, and refuse to accept goods in return, that over a period of time those credits might be cancelled. I would say that would probably be the greatest stimulus to getting countries exporting goods to take payment in goods; because if they do not take payment in goods, after that period of time they would get nothing and they would no longer have the power to demand that payment be made in dollars.
Under a system of that kind I think we would be able to greatly expand both our exports to Europe and our imports from that continent. To complete this paragraph:
To make room for these relatively high-priced imports it would be necessary to impose discriminatory import restrictions.
I have never been able to understand why the price of goods coming in from Britain should be so high. It has always amused me because our friends to our right, the C.C.F., are always extremely critical about price levels in this country and emphatic about the need for controls. Yet here you have a socialist country in which prices are far higher than prices in this country. Why? I have heard it said-and I do not know whether it is correct; I would not like to say that it is correct-that the social services in that country are being maintained by countries paying Britain these high prices, and that the countries that are buying goods from Britain are in reality paying for those services. There may be something in that;

Foreign Exchange Control because the countries who buy these goods pay high prices. The food in England is subsidized and therefore the people there get food at a lower rate. But when we get goods from England we must pay exorbitant prices. For many years I have bought goods that were made in England. Goods that I used to be able to buy quite reasonably-for instance, shirts like the one I have on-could be bought for $3. Now one must pay anywhere from $6.50 to $10 for the same shirt.
I have a nephew who was in the navy. He was in Ottawa last year and he bought a suit of clothes and an overcoat which cost him around $75. He said that if he had bought that suit and coat in England they would have cost him $120. He was going right back to England, yet he bought that suit and overcoat in Ottawa. Why? I think that is something which needs explaining and investigation, because if Britain is keeping her price levels so high that she cannot compete with other countries, then of course she has to accept a certain amount of responsibility for that situation. But even if for some reason or other Britain cannot keep her prices down we are faced with these alternatives. Suppose we make a gift. If we make a gift, we lose the goods of which we make the gift. If we make a loan, we stand a good chance of never being repaid, because the history of international loans has never been a happy one. If we make a loan, we are likely to lose that loan. If, on the other hand, we export goods to Britain and bring goods back, even at a high price, we could very well subsidize those goods which we bring back into this country to bring them down to the price level of Canada. We did that during wartime and again in order to maintain the price ceiling in this country. We imported goods, subsidized them, and sold them at the price level in this country. Surely, if we could carry out a policy of that kind in war, it could be done in peacetime.
The minister might say, well if the British price is 10 per cent higher, then it will cost us 10 per cent. In other words, we would be getting back at least 90 per cent of the value of our export. If we make a gift we get nothing. If we make a loan we are in danger of losing it all. At least we would get paid for 90 per cent of the exports we sent to that country. I am suggesting that it would be good business to import goods, even if we have to pay 10 per cent more than we should, subsidize them, and sell them at the current price in this country. It would be good business because it would help to maintain our production at a high level, and in the long run I do not think there is any doubt that we would benefit by business of that kind. I am 
hoping that eventually Britain will find it possible to bring her price levels down.

speechtext:
I notice that the report does mention this question of discrimination. It says:
To make room for these relatively high-priced imports it would be necessary to impose discriminatory import restrictions.
Well, if we have signed an agreement that outlaws action of that kind, an action that is necessary to keep our economy in a state of flux, the quicker we get out of it the better.
I would say it is evident that the shortage of dollars in Europe is not going to be solved in the near future. I know that many people were hopeful that ERP would solve the shortage of dollars, and by 1952 Europe would be on its feet and in a position to pay for imports from the west with dollars. Well, anybody who has read the interim report of the organization for European economic recovery will realize that there is very little chance of that, or that by 1952 Europe will be in that happy position. I read the report through. I hold in my hand a summary of the report made by the London Economist, dated January 1949, and it puts it far better than I can put it; therefore I shall read what the Economist has to say regarding this report. It is as follows:
It is in discussing the nineteen nations' estimate of their future trade that the officials of the OEEC have most firmly dispelled the idea that a complete solution can be found by 1952. In the first place, the governments themselves have produced estimates which leave a deficit of a billion dollars, largely with the western hemisphere, in western Europe's trading account for 1952. But the interim report questions whether the nations can achieve the scale of exports they have proposed. For instance, to reach the target for exports of $12 billion in 1952, the nations would need among other things to increase their exports to South America by $1 billion above the present level, a step which would seem to entail capturing half the United States' South American markets. Similarly, the increased exports to the United States itself would need to rise to $2-1 billion compared with $1-5 billion sent there in 1938. It is true that the United States is buying more abroad-50 per cent more in 1948 than in 1938-but western Europe's share in American imports has fallen from 23 per cent to 13 per cent. All in all the report concludes that it is impossible to put the level of visible and invisible exports in 1952 above $10 billion, and the deficit is likely to be nearer $3 billion than $1 billion. And even this revised figure demands prodigious efforts-an increase of 40 per cent above the present level of visible exports and the turning of an invisible deficit of $750 million in 1947 into a favourable balance of $1,300 million in 1952.
In concluding the summary the Economist had this to say:
It has often been insisted in these columns that
there were two elements in the dollar shortage_a
European problem and an American problem. This

Is now clear for all the world to see. If Europe, after doing what it can, will still have a deficit of $3 billion, somebody will have a surplus of $3 billion. The one cannot be removed without the other. Certainly the debtors cannot, by taking thought and drawing up plans, remove their deficit unless the creditors will also take thought-and perhaps even draw up plans-about their surplus. The next stage should be a Marshall plan for the creditors.
Perhaps that may sound rather humorous, but I believe there is a lot of sound thought behind the suggestion. That is the point we emphasized time and again during the discussion of the Bretton Woods agreement in this house. We emphasized the point time and again that balancing international trade was the responsibility of two nations. It was the responsibility of the creditor nation just as much as it was the responsibility of the debtor nation, because unless the creditor nation was willing to accept goods in payment the debt could not be paid.
In view of the fact that we are told it is probable that these European nations will still face a deficit of around $3 billion by 1952, it is high time that greater consideration was given to dealing with this problem. As I say, the London Economist emphasizes the need for a Marshall plan for the creditor nations. By the time that the present one has run out in 1952, the production of all European nations will probably have reached approximately their maximum output, and then we must organize our own internal economy to such a degree that we shall be willing to accept the goods that these countries are anxious to send to us. That being so, it is quite evident that the real problem is still ahead. We think we have quite a large problem on our hands at the present time, a problem that unfortunately we have looked upon as a temporary one; but now we realize that it will be a problem that will be with us for many years, and therefore we should look to the future and take steps to deal with it.

However, that is immaterial. Times have changed. Now we see the minister trying to build up the thought in this country that there is a considerable amount of American money coming in.
However there is in Canada, I believe, considerable concern as to the effect the maintenance of the artificial value of our Canadian dollar is having not only upon the inflow of capital into this country, which will be used for purposes of development, but also in respect of the loss of our export trade.
I was going to repeat something the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) said, when he referred to page 6 of the report of the foreign exchange control board. However, I shall leave that out for the moment. I would, however, like to read from page 10 of the report of that foreign exchange control board for 1948, where it states:
The most important change in Canada's commodity trade in 1948 was in the geographical distribution of our exports. The destination in Canadian commodity exports in pre-war and in recent years has been as follows:
I shall exclude the United States figures, although they show that the average from 1935 to 1939, as compared with the 1948 figure, is in the nature of an increase of 13 per cent. However, in those areas in which our great export market is to be found, the market which we as Canadians must maintain if we are going to be a prosperous country-and I am referring to the British isles and the sterling area as a whole-there is shown a very marked decrease. This is more particularly emphasized when one considers that in the 1935-39 period commodity and farm prices were lower than as indicated in the 1948 export figures.
We find that in the 1935-39 period we exported to the United Kingdom 37 per cent 
of our exports, whereas in 1948, in spite of the increased costs of all supplies sold to the British isles, we were down to 23 per cent. In the total sterling area and ERP countries we decreased our exports from 63 per cent in the 1935-39 period to 50 per cent in 1948, or a reduction of practically one-third. And this notwithstanding the fact that in the earlier period prices were much lower.
To me, as one who thinks of the future prosperity of Canada, those figures are most significant. They should give reason for thought to everyone who wants to see our farmers have a market for their goods and our factories a market for their manufactured articles. These figures prove that we have lost a certain amount of trade in the last few years. In spite of the glowing remarks this afternoon by the minister concerning the tremendous dollar volume of trade, it does seem to me that in the last year or so this government, seeing our market slipping away from us, might certainly have given consideration to a barter deal, if you like- some kind of deal. And in this I believe I am following up what was said by the hon. member for Acadia whereby under such an arrangement we in this country would have bought steel, electrical equipment, coal and many other commodities from the British isles, commodities which they have exported to countries behind the iron curtain, with which they have made trade agreements running up to ten-year periods, and supplies of which there has been a shortage in Canada.
We now find ourselves in the position where, with the exception of the wheat agreement, we have only three short-term agreements left with the British isles. I say this situation can be traced to the policy of the government in having placed a fictitious value on the Canadian dollar. It is true that this afternoon the minister said that, by placing our dollar at a 10 per cent discount, purchases from the United Kingdom would have been 10 per cent higher in cost. At the same time, in view of the circumstances, it would have been of much greater advantage to Canada if the British had had 10 per cent greater purchasing power with their pound, and such a condition would have been more beneficial to us.
I consider the recent report of the foreign exchange control board, that for the year 1948, is evidence of the fact that this supposedly non-political board, which parliament is asked to continue in office for a further two years, is aware of the adverse effect of the artificial value of our dollar.
What they are trying to do in this report is to allay the growing concern of the Canadian people by presenting only a part of the

facts so far as the inflow of capital from the United States is concerned. In its report for the year 1948 the foreign exchange control board, in its reference to the inflow of capital from the United States, has confined its report to capital for investment in Canadian properties or business and the increase in book value of United States direct investments in Canada. This method of conveying a false impression to this parliament and to the country is not in accordance with the known facts as to the inflow and outflow of capital, and is a departure which can be justified only on the ground of political expediency.
In the reports to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) of the foreign exchange control board in the past, this parliament and the Canadian people were given a true picture which included not only capital coming to the country for direct investment in plants, but as well the net result of sales and purchases of securities between Canada and other countries. In the report of the foreign exchange control board under date of March 1, 1946, the facts in connection with the movement of capital were dealt with in this way, and I refer to pages 27 and 28 of the report dealing with capital inflows:
In the later years of the war, the inflow of capital to Canada from the United States became an important source of exchange. The inflow took the form mainly of the purchase of securities by United States investors.
That is what the minister stated this afternoon.
The movement first become marked in 1943 when gross sales of outstanding securities for United States dollars amounted to nearly $200 million, or almost twice the total in 1942. While there was some falling off in 1944, the total for the year still exceeded $100 million, and in 1945 rose again to more than $200 million.
That report, with all of the facts in connection with the inflow of capital, was put out in 1946 four months before the parity action of the government when Canada established an artificial value of our dollar. In this connection I might say that the report of the Bank of Canada this year is in an unprecedented form completely different from what it has been in previous years. It does seem to me that the powers that be in the Bank of Canada have tried to make this report more difficult to understand than it was before. There was a true report in 1946 of all facts in connection with the inflow of capital, four months before the parity action of the government. The foreign exchange control board report for 1948, dealing with the inflow of capital, does not follow the practice followed in the past of giving all the facts, but rather confines itself to capital inflow for direct investment purposes in Canadian properties or business, and
Foreign Exchange Control then reaches an all-time high for political reports when it states as follows on page 22:
It is apparent from the above table that the factors which operated to reduce the purchase of publicly issued Canadian securities by United States investors in recent years have not acted as a deterrent to the provision of very large amounts of risk capital for direct investment in Canadian business.
You will notice that in the Bank of Canada's report they do not tell us how much of this money was brought into Canada for, as they say, direct investment in Canadian business. In other words, they do not break it down to tell us what kind of business this money was invested in in Canada. In this connection the Minister of Finance stated this afternoon that there was no difficulty in bringing in a great deal of money from the United States, but I recall very well that last spring a man from Texas wanted to bring in $10 million for oil development in Alberta. I went to see Mr. Graham Towers and Mr. Donald Gordon of the Bank of Canada, and as far as I know I explained the circumstances and the situation as to this man bringing in this large sum of United States funds. I arranged for an interview for him with these officials whereby any difficulties that appeared on the surface might be overcome, and this large sum of money brought in for development in the west.
As a result of the interviews that were had at a later date with the officials of the Bank of Canada, this man from Texas decided that Canada was not a safe place to bring his money because the restrictions that were placed on him were so great that he could not take the chance. We lost that opportunity to get a very large sum of money for development purposes.
The paragraph which I have just read from the 1948 report of the foreign exchange control board states that risk capital from the United States has not been retarded in coming into Canada by reason of the dollar parity. It certainly is retarded by reason of the dollar parity, and it is retarded to a greater degree by the restrictions that are placed on money brought into Canada by the bureaucrats of the Bank of Canada and the foreign exchange control board. The figures given in the report are misleading, and they do not take into account the great forward movement of the development which can be expected in Canada with the influx of risk capital directed to this country where there is a chance of reward for those people who send their money into the country. Everyone familiar with this type of capital knows that it has dried up through recent years in comparison with what it would have been without government interference. The summary under the report of capital influx is, in my opinion, very misleading.

In 1947 we had an outflow of capital from Canada amounting to about $18 million, in spite of the figures that appear in the report of the foreign exchange control board. That report does not show this result, but it is shown by the figures of the bureau of statistics. In the first eleven months of 1948 the outflow of capital amounted to $17-6 million. Yet the minister talks, as he did very glibly this afternoon, of all the risk money coming into Canada. When we get into committee I think he should produce figures to show just how he arrives at that conclusion, and just how much of that money was put into bricks and mortar.
Here is the case of a board acting under power and authority delegated by this parliament, and this resolution asks that we delegate that power for a further period of two years. The minister gave no reasonable statement as to why a period of two years was selected, but it does seem to me this board has just dug itself in and proposes to stay dug in. Instead of the one-year period they have had up to the present, they now ask for two years and sixty days so they can be sure of their jobs for an extended period of time. The foreign exchange control board submit to this parliament, through the Minister of Finance, a report prepared from a political angle by a supposedly non-political board in order to justify its actions in the past; and I say that without reservation. As one who has been interested in the question of exchange for some years, who as a young man came back from the first war and served in New York in the foreign exchange branch of one of the Canadian banks, I think I know a little about exchange. At a later date I shall

have something to say about the size of the staff required to carry out the work of this board. I do submit, Mr. Speaker, that the the political complexion of the 1948 report of the foreign exchange control board is something that goes far beyond any powers ever conferred upon that board or ever intended to be exercised by the board at the time parliament established it in the first place.
There is one other aspect of this report which transcends even the injection of politics, and which in effect strikes at the very root of our parliamentary system of government. I refer to what is apparently becoming a practice in this country of boards and commissions, acting under powers delegated by parliament, actually laying down government policy. This is one of those boards. Very often you see Donald Gordon or Graham Towers or somebody else making speeches that should be made by the minister in this house, just as we find officials of the Department of Finance going around making speeches about things which later become government policy. It would not surprise one if the article in this evening's Citizen about a budget leak is not a true statement.
The objections I have raised already to this report indicate in no uncertain terms the bureaucratic domination of the government by the foreign exchange control board. The report of the Bank of Canada for 1948 is another glaring example. It is in a form entirely different from the reports of other years. I remember saying two years ago that the report of the foreign exchange control board was made up in such a way that, while it may not have been intended to actually deceive members of parliament, it did get them all muddled up so they could not find anything at all in it. This inroad of bureaucratic domination, which is becoming more evident all the time, calls for this parliament to exercise its responsibility to the Canadian people and call a halt to the powers given this department and this government.
This afternoon the minister said something in reference to the gold bonus. I had not intended to touch on that subject at all. I think the minister well knows that the gold mining industry has no desire to be a bonused industry in Canada. In the past they have fought their own battles, and the troubles with which they have been beset during the last few years have been brought upon them by the actions of this government. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) knows as well as I do that when this government needed gold during the war, before the United States came in, he was one of the ministers who approached the gold mining people and asked them to

The party would adopt that favourite if somewhat clumsy description used by hon. members up until today, "to let the

This much we can say, that from the suggestions made by the opposition this afternoon one would gather that the remedy is ^n automatic, selfadjusting, Drew's patent dollar. My own opinion is that, if he were fortunate enough to secure office, after he had been in office about three or four years these dollars would have about as much value as Bennett's buggies.
He asserts that the Progressive Conservative party says that is the way they want it. If they ever succeed, it will mean a good deal to a number of chosen people in Toronto. It will mean joy in the brokerage rooms, but it will mean hardship in the kitchens.

Since the kitchens outnumber the board rooms about a thousand to one, I suggest that in a democracy they are far more important.
There are two possible explanations for our friend's espousal of the present policy. I assume it is honestly advanced as a solution of a difficult problem, the existence of which no one denies; that is one thing. If, on the other hand, it is cynically advanced to satisfy those who give to their party its greatest political support, then that is another matter entirely. If it is honestly advanced, the kindest thing I can say for it at the present time is that they are not thinking this problem through. If it is cynically advanced, there are in the dictionary no words I could possibly use to apply to that particular policy.
I think we can sum up the effect of the policy by saying it will increase the price of both gold and oranges. As everyone in this house knows or should know, a few very powerful people in this country, particularly in my own province, are in the gold-selling business and, as a useful sideline, they run political parties. As everyone also knows, a great many people in this country, undoubtedly the majority of the people in this country, are in the orange-buying line, particularly if they have young children to feed. If you balance the effect of this policy, you will see it means greater wealth for those citizens who happen to be in the gold-producing business and heavier budgets for those citizens who happen to be buying oranges and imports from the United States.
I do not suggest for a moment that these two groups of citizens do not overlap. Gold

miners and their supporters, their political spokesmen, also have children and they do buy oranges. I think a word of commendation may be due to them for their willingness to pay an additional ten per cent or whatever it may be for the oranges that come from the United States, provided that they get an additional ten per cent or whatever it might be for the fine ounce of their gold. In the political language of some of my friends opposite, this is known as equality of sacrifice.
Our friends might say that may be a very narrow view of the matter; it may even be a distorted view. A dollar that was officially worth perhaps ninety cents in United States funds, would help not only the gold mining boys on Bay Street and St. James Street-

-they say it would help a lot of other people in the export business. It would enable Canadians to compete with their United States rivals because Canadians could offer their products at ten per cent, or whatever percentage it turned out to be, cheaper. They could undersell the United States competitor and they would pay their operating costs in the depreciated Canadian dollars, including of course what has already been pointed out to this house, the big item of labour costs. There would be no suggestion of a compensatory rise in wages so that the worker's family could meet the increased price of oranges, coal and other imported goods they need. That would ruin everything; after all, a company executive would also be confronted with higher coal costs and higher prices for oranges. So it would be a matter of equality of sacrifice and share and share alike.
It would seem that this is the proper place to mention the small point of percentage of income required for living costs. I think that what we have failed to grasp up till now-and, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be denied -is that when you impoverish the Canadian dollar you impoverish the Canadian worker and the Canadian farmer.
Let us examine for a moment this idea of Canadian competition. At first it sounds highly attractive. With a ninety-cent dollar we could step into the markets of the world and undersell the Americans who would have to quote in one-hundred-cent dollars. At least, we could do that in cases where the Canadian firm was independent, or where the Canadian producer was not forbidden by his head office to export, or where the American head office had figured it would be good business to shift its export operations to the Canadian subsidiary. There we are with Canadian-

produced goods entering world markets with a ten per cent price advantage over American goods.
I am sure that by now members of this house are beginning to murmur to themselves that the competition is not entirely American. There is British, Scandinavian and Swiss competition; and what is more, on top of all that we are beginning to get a little bit of Japanese and German competition. That is all quite true; I shall deal with it in just a moment, and explain why the result of other competition makes still more questionable the proposition put forward by the opposition.
For the moment, let us adhere to the American competition which is, after all, the big competition in the free markets of the world.
We would have, let us say, something like a ten per cent advantage over our American competitors; but for almost everything we export, for the raw materials that form the bulk of our sales abroad, there is a world price set daily on the commodity markets in New York, or established by private negotiations between the big producers and the big consumers. These world prices are established in American dollars which are, after all, the world currency. Let me ask my friend for an honest answer to this question: Would that price in American dollars for, say, copper or lead or newsprint, be affected one whit by the process of devaluing our dollar? Or would it simply mean that the Canadian producers of these commodities would get a higher profit in terms of Canadian dollars, provided their wage rates stayed down, despite the higher living costs which devaluation would impose upon the wage earners?
Then, to meet the objections that have been raised by the champions of the debased dollar, let us turn to the exporters of Canadian manufactured goods for whom the hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram) attempted to say a few words. They are having a hard time of it today. Let us consider their case as sympathetically as we can. They are pioneering for Canada as a world trader in new and distant fields. Will the ninety-cent dollar help them to market their finished goods against their competitors not only from the United States but from every other industrialized country in the world?
I ask the house this question: Will it help them to sell Coleman lamps in South Africa, or Moffat stoves in Bolivia, or O'Keefe's beer in Pakistan, to mention only three of our major exporters and to keep it as close to home as possible for gentlemen opposite? Of course the answer is no. The trouble with ninety per cent of the markets which would
Foreign Exchange Control normally be open to Canadian producers of finished goods is not a shortage of cash but a shortage of the right kind of cash. It would not matter particularly to importers in most countries if they could get a bargain in terms, of Canadian dollars as against American dollars. They have not either kind of dollars and they simply could not buy on dollar terms. One after another Great Britain, Sweden, South Africa and Mexico have run out of dollars, any kind of dollars, and so they have closed their doors to imports of goods for which the sellers required payment in dollars. This, as my friends well know or should know but refuse to admit, is our dilemma today as a trading nation, as a nation which must trade abroad to maintain prosperity. If any problem surmounts party lines, I think this one does. But what have my friends to offer? Have they any sort of solution? So far, they have not suggested a solution.

When I say exporters, you will realize that I mean not those dealers in essential raw products to whom a devalued dollar would mean an automatic increase in price; I mean those others who send their finished or processed goods abroad to compete in the open market against similar goods from other countries, on the bases of price, quality and Canadian standards of fair dealing.
These estimable firms have an active organization called the Canadian exporters association. They have a first-class trade paper known as the Canadian Exporter. I have yet to learn, Mr. Speaker, that either this organization or its trade paper has endorsed the devaluation which our friends across the way are advancing as the salvation of these very exporters. They have not done so, in spite of the fact that in a handful of dollar markets, and just a handful, and I can name them, Venezuela, Panama, Haiti, the Dominican Kepublic, Cuba, devaluation might help. Their trade paper, which takes a realistic approach, has not argued for devaluation, as have the Bay Street gold miners, which, to put it as kindly as I know how, will never advocate a policy, or force a policy upon its spokesmen, if that policy runs counter to the interest of those who own the mines.
This is one of those occasions, Mr. Speaker, when I wish that parliamentary practice permitted an hon. member on this side of the house to borrow a weapon with which our democratic processes equip our opponents.
I wish it were possible somehow to move a vote of non-confidence in the sincerity of His Majesty's loyal opposition, and to apply it specifically to the single issue of devaluation, which up to the present time is the solitary plank which has miraculously been suspended in mid-air over the site where we should have expected a finished platform to arise long before this time.

It is
rather amusing, Mr. Speaker, to hear the statements of the recent speaker, and it was particularly amusing to hear him quote the opinions of certain industries in Canada. His whole speech can be judged by an example of what he has just said. He mentioned specifically the Coleman lamp company, the Moffat stove company, and one other company, and said that they were happy about the policy of the foreign exchange control board and of the government. As it happens, Mr. Speaker, I hold in my hand a letter from the export manager of the Coleman lamp


company, and I shall quote just one paragraph from it:
We believe that the export trade of the whole world, but particularly also of Canada, is greatly hampered by the many regulations to which our monetary system is subjected. Personally, I can only hope that in the not too distant future the policy of the Canadian government will change in this respect.
Again this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) played the game of the clever fox leading the hounds astray. This afternoon the Minister of Finance discussed the problem of dollar depreciation. The problem is not depreciation; it is convertibility. That is the main problem which is being accentuated by the action of the present administration. We have not got a convertible currency. Let me emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that it is a convertible currency that we need. Until we get a convertible currency we are going to be hamstrung by the actions of others and the actions of our own administration.
I want to go back briefly because I supported the Bretton Woods agreement. I supported it on December 6, 1945, at page 3075 of Hansard, in these terms:
There is, however, the method by which the parity of exchanges shall be fixed, and that appears in article 20, section 4. It merely states that each country shall settle its own parity of its own exchange. That is to me, Mr. Speaker, the crux of the whole question-the method of arriving at parity or of arriving at the currency exchange value in gold of the various members of the agreement. At the present time the huge majority of currencies have a fictitiously high value in terms of the United States dollar, in terms of gold and in terms of the Canadian dollar.
